title: Kirtan

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhajan, the devotional song sung together. Your line was loud. Did you sing one song all the way through, out loud? Day one hundred and thirty-seven.

You walk into a room where people are sitting on the floor, and you don't know a single word of what they're singing. It doesn't matter. At the front, one person sings a line. Then the whole room sings it back. Same line. Then the leader sings again, maybe a little higher, and the room answers again. By the fourth time, you're singing too, without deciding to. By the tenth, the drum has sped up, people are clapping, someone is swaying. And then, all at once, it stops, and the silence is enormous. Today: kirtan.
screen: `ONE VOICE SINGS A LINE.` → `THE ROOM SINGS IT BACK.` → `THEN, ALL AT ONCE, SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Kirtan comes from the Sanskrit kirtana: to praise, to proclaim, to tell out loud. Yesterday's bhajan is a song. Kirtan is more of a conversation. A leader calls, the group answers. It's usually built on the names of the divine, repeated again and again: Rama, Krishna, Govinda, Shiva. The maha-mantra you met on day one hundred and seven, Hare Krishna, Hare Rama, is one of the best-known kirtans in the world. Its most famous champion was Chaitanya, a saint of sixteenth-century Bengal, who led crowds through the streets singing the names and dancing. His followers called it sankirtan, singing together. That spirit traveled a long way; if you've ever seen devotees singing Hare Krishna on a city sidewalk, you've seen its descendants. And the form takes other shapes too. In Maharashtra, a kirtan can be a performance of story and song together, a storyteller with music. Sikhs call their sacred singing kirtan too, in their own tradition. Here's what call and response does. You don't have to know anything. You only have to listen, and give back what you heard. That makes it the most welcoming form of worship there is: a newcomer can join on the second line. It also trains a kind of attention. You can't answer well if you weren't listening. Kirtan often starts slow, builds, speeds up, gets loud, and then stops dead. And in that sudden silence, many people say, is where the kirtan really lands.
screen: `KIRTANA: TO PRAISE OUT LOUD.` · `A LEADER CALLS, THE ROOM ANSWERS.` · `CHAITANYA: SINGING IN THE STREETS.` · `SLOW, FAST, LOUD, THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Let's try one. When you hear a line, answer it back, out loud if you can, inside if you can't. Om namah shivaya. Om namah shivaya. Once more. Om namah shivaya. Now a different call: Hare Krishna, Hare Rama. Hare Krishna, Hare Rama. If you'd rather, just listen to the calls and feel the answer rise. Then let it stop, all at once, and sit in the silence. That silence is part of the kirtan. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan. Praising out loud, together: a leader calls the names of the divine, the room answers, and it ends in silence. Today's word.
Your line: call, answer. Today, in one conversation, listen all the way to the end before you answer, and give back what you actually heard. Day one hundred and thirty-seven.

howItsDone: At a kirtan, a leader sings a line, often a divine name or mantra such as Hare Krishna, and the group sings it back, usually with harmonium, drums and cymbals, building in speed and volume before ending in silence.

original.note: Sanskrit kīrtana: praising, proclaiming, reciting aloud.

trapdoor: what it means: praising out loud together: a leader calls, the room answers, and the silence at the end is part of it.

what a scholar hears: kīrtana appears among the nine forms of bhakti in the Bhagavata Purana (7.5.23); Chaitanya's sixteenth-century nama-sankirtana movement shaped Gaudiya Vaishnavism, and Marathi kirtan is a distinct narrative form.
